Volume 10 · Chapter 07

Brownian motion and Ito calculus

Graduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v10-c06

By the endDerive stochastic differentials and explain quadratic variation.

Explain why a continuous price needs a different chain rule

Capability. Construct the square-integrable Itô integral from trading-like sums, prove Brownian quadratic variation with a specified convergence mode, derive the scalar Itô formula under explicit regularity, and solve and interpret the constant-coefficient geometric Brownian model. The immediate prerequisite is finite binomial replication: choose a position using current information, then earn its gain over the next interval. We also use ordinary differential calculus, convergence modes, and measure, conditional expectation and martingales.

Rill's analyst continuously adjusts an exposure to a fluctuating signal W. Ordinary calculus suggests that the cumulative gain ∫W dW is WT²/2. A ledger that selects each exposure before the next price move gives a different answer. The missing term is not a fee or a forecast error. It comes from squared increments that remain material as the observation interval shrinks. We first build the information and limit arguments needed to resolve this discrepancy; symbols such as (dW)² = dt will then summarize a theorem.

Time is measured in years, W in square roots of years, and asset prices in fictional currency units (CU). Thus a drift in dX = a dt + b dW has units X/year, while b has units X/√year. All numerical observations and model parameters below are original teaching inputs, not market data. A supplied probability law P describes model uncertainty. Calculus alone neither selects a pricing measure nor verifies that actual prices have Brownian dynamics.

1. Brownian motion includes an information restriction

Fix a finite T > 0 and a probability space (Ω, F, P). A filtration (Ft)0≤t≤T records increasing information: Fs ⊆ Ft for s ≤ t. A process H is adapted if Ht is Ft-measurable for each t. We work with complete, right-continuous filtrations, meaning null events are included and Ft = ∩t<u≤TFu for t < T. These conditions concern information, not smoothness of sample paths.

A standard Brownian motion relative to this filtration is an adapted process W with W0 = 0, almost surely continuous paths, and, for every s < t, Wt − Ws independent of Fs with normal law N(0,t−s). Independence from the whole current information set is essential. Independent increments in the natural history do not license adding future prices to F0. The usual completed, right-continuous augmentation of the natural Brownian filtration is an admissible choice. Brownian existence and preservation of its independence under that usual augmentation are foundational results invoked here; they are not established by drawing a continuous curve. The construction route is the consistent Gaussian finite-dimensional laws and a continuous modification; Dembo's probability notes provide the surrounding foundations.

Write ΔW = Wt+h − Wt. Conditional on Ft, its first four moments are 0, h, 0 and 3h². The fourth moment follows by differentiating the normal moment generating function E[euΔW] = eu²h/2 four times at zero. For s ≤ t, Wt = Ws + an independent centered increment, so E[WsWt] = s. In particular, Var(Wt) = t and E[Wt | Fs] = Ws: W is a martingale. Expanding the conditional square also proves that Wt² − t is a martingale.

A typical increment is of scale √h, not h: Var(ΔW/h) = 1/h. This variance calculation explains why a classical slope is the wrong modeling object; it is not, by itself, a proof of nowhere differentiability. We will prove infinite total variation, which is enough to reject ordinary finite-variation integration as a general construction for Brownian trading gains.

2. Quadratic variation: state the partitions and the convergence

Let π = {0=t0<…<tn=T} be a deterministic partition, hi = ti+1 − ti, and |π| = max hi. Define Qπ = Σi(ΔWi)². Independence and the normal moments give the exact identities

E[Qπ] = T,
E[(Qπ − T)²] = Var(Qπ) = 2Σihi² ≤ 2T|π|.

Proof. Each square has mean hi and variance 3hi² − hi² = 2hi². Squares of distinct increments are independent, so their covariance is zero. Summing proves both formulas. Therefore Qπ → T in L², hence in probability, for any sequence of deterministic partitions with mesh tending to zero. This is the quadratic-variation statement used below. For the dyadic partitions with 2m equal intervals, Chebyshev gives P(|Qm−T|>ε) ≤ 2T²/(ε²2m). The sum over m is finite; the first Borel–Cantelli argument from Volume 3 gives Qm → T almost surely. No assertion about every possibly path-dependent partition is inferred from this proof.

The total variation of a continuous path w on [0,T] is the supremum over finite partitions of Σ|Δw|. If it were finite, then on every shrinking-mesh sequence, Σ(Δw)² ≤ max|Δw| · Vartotal(w) → 0 by uniform continuity. On the probability-one set where Brownian paths are continuous and their dyadic squared sums tend to T > 0, this is impossible. Brownian total variation is infinite almost surely. The same argument applies on each fixed nondegenerate interval; a countable collection of rational subintervals establishes the property simultaneously on every interval of positive length.

Finite variation and quadratic variation answer different questions. An ordinary continuously differentiable path has finite variation on a compact interval and zero quadratic variation. A polygon through finitely many observations also has zero quadratic variation when each linear segment is subdivided indefinitely. Adding observations from a Brownian path and subdividing an already fixed polygon are different operations.

Worked example 1 — One finite ledger, three integrals

The supplied sixteen-increment record has T = 1, WT = 1/4, Q = 23/32 and Σ|ΔW| = 3. Direct multiplication gives a left sum L = ΣWtiΔWi = −21/64 and a right sum R = ΣWti+1ΔWi = 25/64. The identities R−L = Q and L+R = WT² hold on every finite real sequence, with no probability assumption.

The average (L+R)/2 = 1/32 is also the ordinary integral of the fixed polygon against itself. For a Brownian model, the Itô integral derived below is (W1²−1)/2 = −15/32 when its terminal value is 1/4. The finite left-sum discrepancy is (1−Q)/2 = 9/64. These endpoint evaluations do not declare that the authored finite record is an actual continuous Brownian path.

If the sixteen increments were independent Gaussian increments of length 1/16, the model would instead imply E[Q] = 1, Var(Q) = 1/8 and E[(L−∫W dW)²] = 1/32. They are distributional statements over all such Gaussian records, not an error bar estimated from this single authored record. Subdividing each fixed polygon segment into m equal parts gives squared sum (23/32)/m → 0, which is an explicit counterexample to confusing interpolation with new Brownian information.

3. Build the integral from positions selected in advance

An elementary predictable process has the form Hs = Σξi1(ti,ti+1](s), where the partition is deterministic and ξi is bounded and Fti-measurable. Its value at zero is immaterial to an integral. The holding is known when its interval begins. Define

It(H) = ∫0tHs dWs := Σiξi[Wt∧ti+1 − Wt∧ti].

Refining a partition without changing holdings leaves this sum unchanged, which also proves linearity after taking a common refinement. Each term has zero conditional future mean. For s between two trading times, split its current increment at s; its holding is already known at s. Every later increment has zero expectation conditional on its own starting information, and the tower property gives zero conditional expectation at s. Thus E[It(H) | Fs] = Is(H): the integral process is a continuous square-integrable martingale.

Itô isometry for elementary processes. On expanding IT(H)², its diagonal terms satisfy E[ξi²(ΔWi)²] = hiE[ξi²]. For i < j, the product ξiΔWiξj is Ftj-measurable. Conditioning the remaining ΔWj makes the cross expectation zero. Bounded holdings ensure the integrability needed for these conditional products. Therefore

E[IT(H)] = 0,
E[IT(H)²] = E[∫0THs² ds] =: ‖H‖H²².

This proof does not assert that random holdings and their earlier price changes are independent. Only the next Brownian increment is independent of information available before it. Unbounded elementary coefficients with E[ξi²] < ∞ enter by truncating each coefficient and using the same norm identity.

The completion and its exact domain

Define H² initially as the closure of bounded elementary predictable processes in L²(Ω×[0,T], P⊗dt); identify processes equal P⊗dt almost everywhere. For H in this closure, choose elementary Hn with ‖Hn−H‖H² → 0. The isometry makes IT(Hn) Cauchy in the complete space L²(P). Its limit defines IT(H). If another approximating sequence is used, the isometry of their difference gives the same limit. Norm continuity preserves the isometry and the zero mean. Applying the construction to 1(0,t]H defines It(H). Conditional expectation is an L² contraction, so passing to the limit in the elementary martingale identities proves the martingale property. Polarization gives E[IT(H)IT(K)] = E∫HK ds. Applying the isometry to 1A1(s,t]H for every A∈Fs also proves the conditional version E[(It−Is)² | Fs] = E[∫stH²du | Fs] by the defining event identities of conditional expectation.

The predictable sigma-algebra is generated by sets A×(s,t], A∈Fs, together with time-zero sets. A predictable process is measurable for this sigma-algebra. We can identify the closure with all predictable H satisfying E∫H² ds < ∞. Here is the density argument. Let C contain the predictable sets whose indicators are in the closure. It contains each generating rectangle and all time-zero sets (the latter are null for P⊗dt). Clip indicator approximations to [0,1], which preserves elementary predictability and cannot enlarge their error. Complements are approximated by 1 minus those approximations. Finite unions are approximated by their pointwise maxima, again elementary on a common partition, with error bounded by the sum of the original errors. Indicators of increasing finite unions converge in L² to the countable-union indicator, since P⊗dt has finite total mass T. Thus C is a sigma-algebra containing the generators, so every predictable indicator belongs to the closure. Finite linear combinations give predictable simple functions; truncation and ordinary simple-function approximation give all predictable L² functions. Conversely, an L² limit of predictable functions has a predictable version by taking a pointwise almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. This proves the identification, with processes always understood modulo P⊗dt null sets.

For continuous adapted H the approximation is more concrete: bounded H has left-step approximations converging pointwise along every continuous path, with a common deterministic bound, so dominated convergence gives convergence in H² directly. Truncation extends the argument when the needed L² domination is available. The MIT lecture on integral construction is a further route through approximation and completion. Mere separate adaptedness without the required process measurability and integrability is not our domain definition.

Why the completed integral has continuous paths

We need more than a terminal random variable. For a continuous square-integrable martingale M, the following maximal bound holds:

E[sup0≤t≤T|Mt|²] ≤ 4E[|MT|²].

Proof of the bound. First sample M at finitely many deterministic times including T and let M* be their maximum absolute value. Partition the event {M*≥λ} by the first sampled crossing. At a crossing time k, conditional Jensen and the martingale property give |Mk| ≤ E[|MT| | Fk]. Multiplying by its crossing indicator and summing gives λP(M*≥λ) ≤ E[|MT|1{M*≥λ}]. Integrating twice the two sides over λ from 0 to R yields E[(M*∧R)²] ≤ 2E[|MT|(M*∧R)]. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the latter and gives E[(M*∧R)²] ≤ 4E|MT|². Let R increase and then take nested dense finite time sets; monotone convergence and continuity prove the displayed bound.

Apply it to I(Hn)−I(Hm) and use the isometry. The sequence is Cauchy in expected squared uniform distance. Choose a subsequence whose expected uniform distances between successive terms are summable; Tonelli makes their sum finite almost surely. Hence this subsequence converges uniformly almost surely to a continuous process. At each fixed time it has the already-defined L² limit. This gives a continuous version, unique up to equality for all times outside one null event. The bound passes to the limit. We henceforth use that version.

A stopping time τ satisfies {τ≤t}∈Ft. The identity It∧τ(H) = It(1(0,τ]H) follows first for stopping times on a finite grid, then by approximating a bounded τ from above on dyadic grids, using the isometry and continuity. The stopped integrand is predictable. For predictable H with ∫H² ds finite almost surely but possibly infinite expectation, stop when this accumulated integral reaches n and construct the compatible square-integrable stopped integrals. Their agreement on overlaps defines a local integral. It is a local martingale: a martingale after such stopping. Its unstopped expectation need not remain zero. Removing stops inside an expectation requires an integrability argument.

Worked example 2 — An adapted integral need not be normal

On [0,1], hold H = 2 until time 1/2, then H = 3W1/2 until time 1. Put U = W1/2 and V = W1−W1/2; U,V are independent N(0,1/2). The integral is I = 2U + 3UV = U(2+3V). Its mean is zero and the isometry gives Var(I) = 4(1/2) + 9E[U²](1/2) = 17/4.

Independence gives E[I⁴] = E[U⁴]E[(2+3V)⁴] = (3/4)[16 + 6(4)(9)(1/2) + 81(3/4)] = 2217/16. A centered normal variable with variance 17/4 has fourth moment 3(17/4)² = 867/16. Thus the integral is not normal. It is the integrator that has normal independent increments; random feedback holdings can change the distribution of accumulated gains.

In contrast, for deterministic square-integrable h(t), elementary integral approximations are centered normal variables with variance ∫hn(t)²dt. Their characteristic functions converge to exp(−u²∫h²/2), while L² convergence implies convergence in distribution. Thus ∫h dW is centered normal with variance ∫h². This argument does not apply when h depends on W.

4. The first integral and the cost of looking ahead

For Hs = Ws, E∫0TWs²ds = T²/2 < ∞. The left-step error is explicit:

E∫0T(Ws−Wπ(s))²ds = Σi∫titi+1(s−ti)ds = ½Σihi².

Here π(s) denotes the left endpoint of s's interval. Algebra on each interval gives 2WtiΔWi = Wti+1² − Wti² − (ΔWi)². Summing, using the integral construction and the proved L² quadratic variation, yields

∫0TWsdWs = ½(WT² − T),
E[∫W dW] = 0, Var(∫W dW) = T²/2.

The same finite identity proves the exact mean-square error of the left sum: E[(Lπ−∫W dW)²] = ½Σhi². Also Var(Lπ) = Σtihi = (T²−Σhi²)/2 by the isometry. The right sum is Rπ = Lπ + Qπ, so it tends to (WT²+T)/2 and has mean T. Its holdings use the next interval's outcome; it is not the same predictable strategy.

For completeness, Cov(WT²,Qπ) = 2Σhi²: in expanding WT², the pairwise distinct-increment products have zero covariance with each increment square, and the diagonal squares supply their variances. Since Rπ = (WT²+Qπ)/2, Var(Rπ) = (T²+3Σhi²)/2. Averaging left and right sums instead gives WT²/2. That symmetric convention is consistent with the Stratonovich integral for this example, but it is not the preselected-holding gain convention proved here. A change of convention must carry its correction term.

5. A scalar Itô formula with controlled errors

We prove the version needed for the next chapter. Let

Xt = x + At + Mt, At = ∫0tasds, Mt = ∫0tbsdWs,

where x is finite and deterministic and a,b are continuous adapted processes on the finite horizon; their local integrals are well defined because each continuous path is bounded on a compact interval. Suppose f(t,x) has a continuous time derivative ft and continuous spatial derivatives fx, fxx, denoted f∈C1,2. Then, almost surely for all t in the horizon,

f(t,Xt) − f(0,x) = ∫0t[ft + asfx + ½bs²fxx](s,Xs)ds + ∫0tbsfx(s,Xs)dWs.

The formula holds up to exit from an open spatial domain on which f is C1,2. If f is regular only for t < T, first apply it on every [0,U] with U < T; taking a limit at maturity needs a separate argument. The broader theorem for merely integrable predictable coefficients and general continuous semimartingales is not proved here. The following bounded proof, followed by localization, covers the continuous coefficients used in our examples and geometric Brownian pricing.

Step 1: approximate the stochastic increments

First take a,b bounded by a deterministic constant C, with continuous paths, and f and its displayed derivatives bounded and uniformly continuous on the time-state region used in the proof. Write bi = bti. On each deterministic interval, ΔMi = biΔWi + ri, where ri = ∫(bs−bi)dWs over that interval. The isometry and dominated convergence give

EΣri² = E∫0t|bs−bπ(s)|²ds → 0,
Σ(ΔAi)² ≤ C²t|π| → 0, EΣ(biΔWi)² ≤ C²t.

Thus the sum of squares of the total errors ri+ΔAi tends to zero in probability, while the base squared sum is bounded in probability. Cauchy–Schwarz, |Σuivi| ≤ (Σui²Σvi²)1/2, makes their cross sums vanish. The same absolute bound works after multiplication by any bounded weights ci. Consequently

Σci[(ΔXi)² − bi²(ΔWi)²] → 0 in probability.

Step 2: weighted quadratic variation

For bounded Fti-measurable weights ki, the variables ki[(ΔWi)²−hi] are martingale differences. Conditioning the later term shows that distinct terms are orthogonal even though their weights may be dependent. Their squared sum expectation is

E[(Σki((ΔWi)²−hi))²] = 2ΣE[ki²]hi² ≤ 2K²t|π|, when |ki|≤K.

Use ci = fxx(ti,Xti) and ki = cibi². The preceding bound and Step 1 reduce the weighted squared-increment sum to Σfxx(ti,Xti)bi²hi, whose pathwise Riemann limit is ∫fxx(s,Xs)bs²ds. Taking ci = 1 also proves Σ(ΔXi)² → ∫b²ds in probability. In particular these sums are bounded in probability; this fact controls the Taylor remainder.

Step 3: the Taylor remainder really disappears

Split f(ti+1,Xi+1)−f(ti,Xi) into its time change at Xi+1 and its spatial change at ti. The time change is ∫titi+1ft(s,Xi+1)ds. Replace it by ft(ti,Xi)hi; the total error is bounded by t times the modulus of continuity of ft at |π|+max|ΔXi|, tending to zero almost surely. A second-order spatial Taylor expansion gives fx(ti,Xi)ΔXi + ½fxx(ti,Xi)(ΔXi)², with summed remainder bounded by

½ωxx(max|ΔXi|) · Σ(ΔXi)² → 0 in probability.

Continuity of X gives max|ΔXi| → 0 almost surely, and Step 2 gives the required boundedness in probability. This argument needs only continuous second spatial derivatives, not a third derivative or a mixed time-space derivative. The finite-variation linear sum tends to ∫fxa ds by pathwise dominated convergence. The martingale linear sum equals ∫fx(π(s),Xπ(s))bsdWs and tends in L² to ∫fx(s,Xs)bsdWs by the isometry. Telescoping the Taylor expansions proves the formula at each fixed t. Intersect the probability-one equality events at rational t; continuity of both sides extends equality to all t.

Step 4: remove artificial bounds by stopping

Stop when |X|, |a| or |b| first reaches n, and, if necessary, before X leaves a compact subinterval of f's open domain. Replace f outside that compact set by a smooth spatial cutoff agreeing with it in a neighborhood of the stopped path. The derivatives are then bounded and uniformly continuous on the compact time interval. Choose n > |x| and stop at the first threshold crossing, including an immediate stop if an initial coefficient already exceeds its bound. On that immediate-stop event set the coefficients at time zero to zero, an immaterial single-time change. The stopped coefficients as1{s≤τ}, bs1{s≤τ} for s > 0 are then bounded and continuous except possibly at the single stopping time. The left approximations used above still converge for dt-almost every s on every path, so all the dominated-convergence and Riemann arguments remain valid. Evaluate the resulting formula at t∧τ; its time integral then also ends at t∧τ. On every path that stays in the open domain through T, continuity makes these stops eventually exceed each fixed time (indeed the whole horizon if the image is a compact subset of the domain). The stopped identities therefore agree with the desired local identity. This removes bounds without asserting convergence of unstopped expectations.

The mnemonic (dW)² = dt now records weighted quadratic variation. The other rules dt·dt = dt·dW = 0 record the vanishing squared-drift and drift-martingale cross sums in Step 1. They are rules for integrated limits, not multiplication of ordinary pointwise derivatives. The Haugh diffusion notes provide further applications; the proof and its narrower continuous-coefficient scope are specified above.

6. Products, covariation and the meaning of drift

For dX = a dt + b dW and dY = c dt + d dW with the same Brownian driver and continuous adapted coefficients, define quadratic covariation along deterministic shrinking partitions by [X,Y]t = lim ΣΔXΔY in probability. Polarization, 2ΔXΔY = (ΔX+ΔY)²−(ΔX)²−(ΔY)², and the proved quadratic-variation result give [X,Y]t = ∫0tbsdsds. Here d is the named diffusion coefficient of Y, not an instruction to differentiate. Applying the scalar formula to (X+Y)², X² and Y² and subtracting proves

d(XY) = X dY + Y dX + d[X,Y]
= (Xc + Ya + bd)dt + (Xd + Yb)dW.

If one process has finite variation, its diffusion coefficient is zero and the cross term vanishes. Multiplication by a deterministic discount factor therefore uses the ordinary product correction, whereas multiplying two risky positions generally does not. A portfolio value identity V = ΔS + βB does not by itself imply dV = ΔdS + βdB. The product rule also contains terms from changing Δ and β. Calling a strategy self-financing means that the rebalancing cash and covariation terms are financed internally so that its gain equation holds; stochastic calculus does not grant this financing condition automatically.

For a constant-coefficient arithmetic diffusion Xt = x+at+bWt, the conditional increment has mean ah and variance b²h exactly. In a state-dependent model, at and bt describe local drift and local diffusion; finite-horizon moments generally require solving the model. Under bounded continuity, the mean increment divided by h tends to at and the conditional squared-increment rate tends to bt² in L¹, using conditional contraction, dominated convergence and the isometry. Statements without these integrability conditions require localization or stronger hypotheses. A nonlinear transformation changes drift through its curvature even when the original drift is zero.

Worked example 3 — Curvature and common-shock exposure

Let Xt = 2+0.4t+0.6Wt, Yt = 3−0.2t+0.5Wt, and Zt = e−tXt². Since ft = −e−tx², fx = 2e−tx and fxx = 2e−t,

dZ = e−t(−X²+0.8X+0.36)dt + 1.2e−tX dW,
d(XY) = (0.4Y−0.2X+0.30)dt + (0.6Y+0.5X)dW.

At t = 1, W = 1/4 gives X = 2.55, Y = 2.925 and Z ≈ 2.392136. Z's drift and diffusion there are approximately −1.509225 and 1.125711. Product drift is 0.96 and product diffusion is 3.03. The product correction 0.30 is essential because both processes respond to the same shock.

Independently, E[X1²] = 2.4²+0.6² = 6.12, so E[Z1] = 6.12/e ≈ 2.251422. E[X1Y1] = 2.4(2.8)+0.6(0.5) = 7.02; multiplying the two means would miss 0.30. Their path quadratic variations over the year are 0.36 and 0.25, with cross variation 0.30. These are distinct from a single observed squared price change.

7. An SDE is an integral equation, and this one can be solved

The notation dSt = μStdt + σStdWt, S0 = s0, means St = s0 + ∫μS ds + ∫σS dW. With finite real constants μ,σ and s0 > 0, define

St = s0 exp[(μ−σ²/2)t + σWt].

Apply the proved formula to f(t,w) = s0exp[(μ−σ²/2)t+σw], using X = W. Its time derivative contributes (μ−σ²/2)S, and its second spatial derivative contributes σ²S/2; together they give μS. Its stochastic coefficient is σS. This directly verifies a continuous adapted solution driven by the given W, which is a strong solution. There is no circular assumption that a solution exists before writing its logarithm.

It is also the unique continuous adapted solution driven by this W and initial value. Put Et = exp[(μ−σ²/2)t+σWt] and Rt = 1/Et. Direct Itô calculation gives dR = (−μ+σ²)R dt − σR dW. For any proposed continuous solution S, the product rule gives d(RS) = RS[μ−μ+σ²−σ²]dt + RS[σ−σ]dW = 0, locally and hence on every finite horizon. Therefore RS = s0 and S = s0E. This is pathwise uniqueness for this specific SDE, not a proof of existence and uniqueness for arbitrary nonlinear SDEs.

The explicit solution is positive. On a compact time interval its continuous path stays away from zero, so the localized formula for log on (0,∞) is valid:

d log St = (μ−σ²/2)dt + σdWt,
log(St/s0) ∼ N((μ−σ²/2)t, σ²t).

The normal exponential moment, obtained by completing the square in the normal density, gives for every real p

E[Stp] = s0p exp[pμt + ½p(p−1)σ²t],
E[St] = s0eμt, Var(St) = s0²e2μt(eσ²t−1).

Conditioning at u ≤ t gives the same moment multiplier over t−u times Sup, by independence of future increments. In particular Nt = e−μtSt is a true square-integrable martingale with E[NT²] = s0²eσ²T. Our maximal bound gives E[supt≤TSt²] ≤ 4e2|μ|Ts0²eσ²T < ∞. This justifies, for example, square integrability of bounded-exposure gains on finite horizons. It does not prove that every local martingale or unrestricted trading gain is a true martingale.

When σ = 0 the solution is the ordinary deterministic growth path. When s0 = 0 the unique solution is identically zero and log is undefined. Negative initial values remain negative mathematically, but are outside the positive-price interpretation. A finite μ may be negative. Even with μ > 0, typical log growth μ−σ²/2 may be negative: a mean price and a median price answer different questions. Model μ is neither automatically a risk-free rate nor a calibrated option-implied quantity.

Worked example 4 — Exact growth and an Euler failure

Use s0 = 80 CU, μ = 0.06/year, σ = 0.30/√year and T = 1 year. Mean log return is 0.015 and log-return variance is 0.09. The median price is 80e0.015 ≈ 81.209045; the mean is 80e0.06 ≈ 84.946924; price variance is approximately 679.559734 CU². For the finite record's endpoint W1 = 1/4, the explicit formula evaluates to 80e0.09 ≈ 87.533943.

The Euler update Ei+1 = Ei(1+μh+σΔWi) uses the left price. At h = 1/4 and the stress increment ΔW = −4√year, its factor is −37/200 and its price is −14.8 CU. The exact exponential update is approximately 24.186065 CU, still positive. This is an extreme authored probe, not a frequency estimate. For any σ > 0 and positive h, a Gaussian increment has a nonzero lower-tail probability of making the Euler factor nonpositive. Smaller time steps can reduce that probability without making it mathematically zero.

8. A reproducible laboratory with analytical error anchors

Download the inputs, standard-library model, reference output, standalone instructions, and four-file hash manifest. Run the script with explicit input and output paths. Rational ledgers are exact; fields ending in _approx are floating approximations. The supplied case preserves the authored sixteen observations, compares their coarser aggregations, and contrasts polygon refinement with exact Gaussian moment identities. No random seed is needed because no random draw is used.

A three-point increment √(3h)Z with P(Z=−1)=P(Z=1)=1/6 and P(Z=0)=2/3 matches Gaussian moments through degree four. Enumerating four independent such increments gives 81 weighted states and exactly reproduces the quadratic-sum and left/right-integral moments used here. It does not reproduce a Gaussian distribution, its tails, or exponential GBM moments. In particular E[(√3 Z)6] = 9, whereas a standard normal sixth moment is 15. This is finite moment cubature, not empirical validation or a convergence proof.

The GBM error calculation uses genuine Gaussian analytical moments, separately from that cubature. For n equal steps h=T/n, Euler terminal En is coupled to the exact terminal ST using the same Gaussian increments. Independence across increments gives

E[En] = s0(1+μh)n,
E[En²] = s0²[(1+μh)²+σ²h]n,
E[STEn] = s0²eμT[1+(μ+σ²)h]n,
E[(En−ST)²] = E[En²]+E[ST²]−2E[STEn].

To verify the cross moment rather than assume it, differentiate E[euΔW] = eu²h/2: E[ΔW eσΔW] = σh eσ²h/2. Therefore each increment's exponential-times-Euler expectation is eσ²h/2[1+(μ+σ²)h]; multiplication and the exact drift exponential give the third formula. In the worked case, n = 4,16,64 gives mean biases approximately −0.037840, −0.009532, −0.002388 CU and coupled mean-square errors 8.044271, 2.002215, 0.499877 CU². These exact model expectations separate weak mean bias from strong path-coupled error. Their square roots, not the MSEs, have price units. The formulas tend to the exact moments as h→0 and make this case's convergence assessable without fitting a line through a few simulated points.

A useful report changes the horizon and coefficients, preserves the information rule, checks the exact identities first, and explains what a numerical comparison can establish. A smooth-looking plot, a single seed, or a decreasing interpolation error cannot establish Brownian existence, infinite variation, empirical Gaussian increments, or reliable hedging in an actual market.

Exercises

  1. Information and a false gain. On [0,1] with the Brownian natural filtration, compare the proposed constant-in-time holding Ht = W1 with Ht = Wt. Both have finite E∫H²dt. Which belongs to the permitted information class? Evaluate the naive finite gain W1ΣΔW and its expectation, and explain why it does not contradict the zero-mean Itô theorem.
  2. Unequal intervals and optimal observation spacing. For times 0,1/8,1/2,1, derive E[Q], Var(Q) and the left approximation's MSE for ∫W dW. Among all deterministic n-interval partitions of [0,T], prove that equal intervals minimize both errors, and give the minima. State exactly which convergence conclusion the variance bound proves.
  3. A distribution audit. Find the distribution of ∫01(1+t)dWt. Then recompute the variance and fourth moment of the two-stage holding in Worked example 2. Explain why applying the deterministic normal-integral rule to the second case fails. Include the degenerate deterministic integrand h=0.
  4. Proof: random weights do not spoil the right orthogonality. For |ki|≤K with ki∈Fti, prove E[(Σki((ΔWi)²−hi))²] = 2ΣE[ki²]hi². Identify precisely where nonanticipation enters. Does the proof remain valid for ki = (ΔWi)²?
  5. Integration by parts. Derive ∫0Tt dWt = TWT−∫0TWtdt. Find its mean, variance and covariance with WT. Justify the covariance using polarization of the isometry, and state the relevant integrability conditions.
  6. A fresh Itô and product calculation. Let Xt = 1−t/4+Wt/2 and Yt = 2+t+Wt/4. Derive d(e−2tX²) and d(XY). At T=2 find E[e−4X2²], E[X2Y2] and [X,Y]2. Explain why multiplying means fails for the product.
  7. Growth, inverse prices and uniqueness. A positive GBM has s0=50, μ=0.02 and σ=0.4. At T=2 find the mean log return, log variance, median, mean and E[1/ST]. Derive d(1/S) and use the chapter's integrating factor argument to justify pathwise uniqueness without assuming that every competing solution is positive.
  8. Prove an error formula and test a boundary. Derive the coupled Euler–GBM cross moment and MSE displayed in the laboratory, and independently calculate their n=4 benchmark for s0=80, μ=0.06, σ=0.30, T=1. If σ=0, what does this MSE reduce to? If also μ=0, what are the Euler bias and MSE? Explain why a negative Euler price is a scheme defect here.
  9. Stopping and honest expectations. For the positive constant-coefficient GBM, prove the chapter's finite-horizon bound on E[sup S²] using the exponential normal moment and the proved maximal inequality. Deduce a bound on E∫0T(HtσSt)²dt when H is predictable and |H|≤L. Identify what this allows you to assert about ∫HσS dW, and what extra work is required if H is merely locally bounded.
  10. Research and numerical critique. A report claims that “the sixteen-point path proves Brownian quadratic variation; linear interpolation improves the proof; fourth-moment matching validates Gaussian tail probabilities; zero local drift guarantees a zero unconditional expected gain; and a positive mean GBM return guarantees positive median growth.” Write a referee response addressing every claim, using at least two explicit formulas or counterexamples from the chapter. Propose a reproducible numerical design that separates theorem, numerical error, model assumptions and empirical evidence. No new statistical testing method is required.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria
  1. Wt is continuous adapted and lies in H² since ∫01E[Wt²]dt=1/2. Its integral is (W1²−1)/2 with mean zero. W1 is unavailable at t<1 and is not adapted or predictable for this filtration, despite E∫W1²dt=1. The naive gain is W1² with expectation 1. It uses hindsight and is outside the theorem's domain. Enlarging information at time zero to reveal W1 also destroys the assumed Brownian independence from current information.
  2. The lengths are 1/8,3/8,1/2, whose squared sum is (1+9+16)/64=13/32. Thus E[Q]=1, Var(Q)=13/16 and left-integral MSE=13/64. For n lengths with sum T, Cauchy–Schwarz gives T²=(Σhi)²≤nΣhi², with equality exactly when all are T/n. Minimum quadratic-sum variance is 2T²/n and minimum left MSE is T²/(2n). A deterministic shrinking mesh proves convergence in L² and probability. Almost-sure convergence needs an additional argument, supplied here for the dyadic sequence by summability; it is not an unrestricted pathwise partition statement.
  3. The deterministic integral is N(0,∫01(1+t)²dt)=N(0,7/3), justified by the deterministic normal-approximation argument. For I=U(2+3V), independent U,V∼N(0,1/2) give E[I]=0, E[I²]=(1/2)(4+9/2)=17/4 and E[I⁴]=(3/4)(16+108+243/4)=2217/16. This differs from 3(17/4)²=867/16, so the integral is not normal. The second holding uses feedback from U; independence of U from its own coefficient 3U was never available. h=0 gives the constant zero, conventionally a degenerate normal with zero variance.
  4. Let Di=(ΔWi)²−hi. Independence gives E[Di|Fti]=0 and E[Di²|Fti]=2hi². For i<j, kiDikj is measurable at tj, so E[kiDikjDj]=0 by conditioning. The diagonal is 2hi²E[ki²]; sum to obtain the identity. Boundedness ensures all products are integrable. The proposed replacement (ΔWi)² is neither bounded nor known at ti; indeed E[(ΔWi)²Di]=3hi²−hi²=2hi², not zero. Truncating a future-dependent weight can fix boundedness without fixing nonanticipation.
  5. The process t has drift 1 and zero diffusion, so d(tWt)=t dWt+Wtdt, with zero covariation. Integrate from 0. Deterministic t and 1 lie in H² on finite [0,T]; the continuous path also makes the ordinary time integral meaningful. The stochastic integral has mean 0 and variance ∫0Tt²dt=T³/3. Since WT=IT(1), polarization gives covariance E[I(t)I(1)]=∫0Tt dt=T²/2. All these moments are finite.
  6. For f=e−2tx², the drift is e−2t(−2X²−X/2+1/4), and diffusion is e−2tX. The product drift is X−Y/4+1/8, diffusion is X/4+Y/2. At T=2, E[X]=1/2, Var(X)=1/2, E[Y]=4 and Cov(X,Y)=(1/2)(1/4)(2)=1/4. Therefore E[e−4X²]=(3/4)e−4≈0.0137367292, E[XY]=(1/2)(4)+1/4=9/4 and [X,Y]2=1/4. Multiplying means omits the common Brownian-shock covariance. Pathwise quadratic covariation and terminal covariance coincide numerically in this constant-coefficient case, but they have different definitions.
  7. μ−σ²/2=−0.06. Thus log mean is −0.12, log variance 0.32, median 50e−0.12≈44.346022, and mean 50e0.04≈52.040539. Taking p=−1 gives E[1/S2]=(1/50)e0.28≈0.0264625962 CU−1. The derivatives of 1/s give d(1/S)=(−μ+σ²)(1/S)dt−σ(1/S)dW=0.14(1/S)dt−0.4(1/S)dW. For uniqueness define R from the explicit exponential alone, which is always positive. Multiplying any competing continuous solution by R makes every drift and stochastic term cancel, regardless of its sign. Hence RS is the fixed initial value 50; this establishes both equality and positivity of the competing solution. It avoids presupposing a logarithm for that solution.
  8. For an increment ΔW∼N(0,h), E[eσΔW(1+μh+σΔW)]=eσ²h/2[1+(μ+σ²)h]. Multiply the n independent factors and include s0²e(μ−σ²/2)T to obtain the cross moment. Expanding the squared terminal difference yields the MSE formula. For n=4 the exact second moment is 6400e0.21≈7895.539584, Euler second moment is 6400(1.015²+0.0225)⁴≈7860.310836, and cross moment is 6400e0.06(1.0375)⁴≈7873.903074, giving MSE≈8.044270660 CU². When σ=0, both variables are deterministic, so MSE=s0²[(1+μT/n)n−eμT]². If μ is also zero, Euler is exact, with zero bias and MSE. With positive initial price, the verified exact GBM stays positive; a negative Euler value therefore belongs to the discretization, not to this exact model.
  9. Nt=e−μtSt is a martingale by the conditional normal exponential moment, with E[NT²]=s0²eσ²T. Pathwise sup S²≤e2|μ|Tsup N². The maximal inequality gives the bound 4e2|μ|Ts0²eσ²T. Hence E∫(HσS)²dt≤L²σ²T·4e2|μ|Ts0²eσ²T, finite (zero if σ=0). The predictable integrand lies in H², so its integral is a continuous square-integrable martingale with mean zero. Local boundedness alone produces only localized bounds whose constants may grow with the stop; to remove stops in expected gains, prove global square integrability or another suitable uniform-integrability argument. It is not enough that each realized path has a finite local bound.
  10. Illustrative response. The finite path has Q=23/32 rather than 1 and supplies an algebraic example, not a limiting theorem. Fixed-polygon refinement gives Q/m→0, whereas Brownian deterministic-grid Q converges to T in L² with variance 2Σh². Three-point cubature has sixth moment 9 instead of the normal 15; matching four moments cannot validate tails or exponential moments. A local integral need not have the unstopped zero-mean property without integrability; Volume 3's stopping example already warns against exchanging expectation and a limit. Positive μ does not imply μ−σ²/2>0: Exercise 7 has positive mean price growth and negative median growth. A reproducible study would preserve inputs, conventions and code; check exact ledger identities; use several nested Gaussian grids with explicitly coupled increments if simulation is added; compare mean bias and path MSE with the analytical GBM formulas; separately check positivity stresses and moment-cubature limitations; and treat actual data provenance, observation noise, dependence and tail behavior as additional empirical questions. Rubric, 10 points: one point for correctly diagnosing each of five claims; two for correct explicit quantitative counterarguments; two for a reproducible error comparison separating grid, sampling and model issues; one for a precise statement of what remains unproved or empirically untested. Other designs earn full credit if they meet these criteria without claiming simulation proves a theorem.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back prompt. Explain to a colleague why a left-endpoint exposure has zero expected Brownian gain, why its squared increments still accumulate, and how both facts can coexist in d(W²)=2W dW+dt. Name the integrability and information conditions before interpreting a strategy's expected profit.

Answer standard. A holding measurable before the next increment can be pulled out of its conditional expectation, leaving zero. Its product with that increment nevertheless has nonzero second moment. Independent Gaussian squared increments have total mean T and variance tending to zero, producing quadratic variation T. Therefore W²'s change includes the finite-variation drift dt and its compensated part W²−t is a martingale. Completion preserves zero mean only in the stated square-integrable domain; localization by itself does not guarantee the unstopped expectation. Full credit requires the timing, variance, correction and domain, rather than just reciting (dW)²=dt.

After one week, without notes: (a) at T=2 with eight equal Gaussian intervals, find Var(Q) and the left ∫W dW approximation MSE; (b) for dS/S=0.04dt+0.4dW find log drift; (c) explain what fails if a holding uses the next increment; (d) state which existence and generality results were invoked rather than proved.

Retention answers. (a) 2T²/n=1 and T²/(2n)=1/4; (b) 0.04−0.16/2=−0.04/year; (c) the holding need not be measurable at the increment's start, so the zero conditional-mean and orthogonality proofs fail; (d) Brownian existence and preservation of independence under the usual filtration augmentation were invoked. The chapter proves predictable-L² density, the integral on its closure, its continuous version, the continuous-coefficient localized scalar formula and explicit GBM existence/pathwise uniqueness. It does not prove general nonlinear SDE existence, general Girsanov, martingale representation, or the full semimartingale calculus.

Sources and next step

Further study: Dembo, Probability Theory, sections 8.1–8.3 and 9.1–9.2, for process construction, Brownian continuity and filtration/maximal-inequality foundations; MIT 15.070J Lecture 15 (2013), for integral approximation; and Haugh, Introduction to Stochastic Calculus for Diffusions (2013), sections 1–5, for a finance-oriented method route. These are scoped method references, not empirical support for a price law. The ledgers, proof organization, numerical case, exercises and solutions here are original. Broader existence and change-of-measure results require further study as explicitly identified above.

The next chapter, Black–Scholes and risk-neutral valuation, adds a financing model, a self-financing replication argument and a carefully specified change of probability law. The Itô correction is now available; an option-pricing conclusion still needs those additional economic and mathematical assumptions.
